title: Symphony No. 3 in E-flat major, “Rhenish”
hook: Schumann’s new life on the Rhine, with a solemn visit to Cologne Cathedral at its heart.

painting.title: Ideal View of Cologne Cathedral from the South-West
painting.pairingNote: The cathedral as it was meant to look when finished, painted while it still stood half-built; Schumann saw the unfinished building in 1850, and its memory runs through the solemn fourth movement.

facts: In September 1850 Robert and Clara Schumann moved to Düsseldorf on the Rhine, where he had become the city’s director of music. The welcome was warm and he was in high spirits. He wrote this symphony in about five weeks, in November and December 1850.

He visited Cologne and its cathedral, then still unfinished, in late September and again in early November. The fourth movement was first headed “in the character of the accompaniment to a solemn ceremony”. It is often linked with the ceremony that made the Archbishop of Cologne a cardinal on 12 November 1850, but Schumann’s diary suggests he was not there.

He conducted the first performance in Düsseldorf in February 1851, and the audience applauded between the movements. It was the last symphony he composed. It is called No. 3 only because his D minor symphony of 1841 was revised and published later, as No. 4.

It has five movements instead of four, and “Rhenish” is not his title: the name goes back to his first biographer, Wilhelm Joseph von Wasielewski. Schumann removed the descriptive headings before publication, wanting listeners to hear the music on its own terms.
bigPicture.inOneLine: a striding, sunlit opening (I), a rolling country dance (II), a quiet interlude (III), a solemn ceremony under high vaults (IV), a festive finale (V).

movements.heading: Lebhaft
movements.summary: No introduction: the whole orchestra plunges straight into a broad, striding theme. It is written in three, but it swings across the bar lines as if in slow, wide beats of two. The movement is in [[sonata-form|sonata form]], with a short, wistful second theme, a long development and a horn call that announces the return.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 1, everyone
mainIdeas.description: a heroic, upward-surging tune whose accents fall across the beat.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 2, oboes
mainIdeas.description: a gentle, sighing melody in G minor.

mainIdeas.name: The horn call
mainIdeas.description: Theme 1 stretched out into long notes, played by the four horns.

notice: Try counting three beats in the opening tune. The music fights the count: its long notes push across the bar line, which gives the theme its sense of huge, striding steps.
Listen for the horns at about two-thirds of the way through. Their long-note version of the theme sounds like the main theme seen from far away.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: Giulini was music director of the Los Angeles Philharmonic from 1978 to 1984, and this recording was released in 1982. His tempos are broad, especially in the first movement. On the Spotify album the symphony is tracks 1–5, followed by the *Manfred* Overture.

movements.heading: Scherzo: Sehr mäßig
movements.summary: Called a scherzo but marked “very moderate”, this is really a [[landler|ländler]], a country dance in three. Its rolling tune, first in the lower strings and bassoons, keeps coming back in new dress. Many listeners hear in it the flow of the Rhine.

mainIdeas.name: The ländler
mainIdeas.description: a sturdy, rolling melody in C major, low in the orchestra.

mainIdeas.name: The middle section
mainIdeas.description: a softer tune in A minor in the horns and woodwinds, over a long-held note.

movements.heading: Nicht schnell
movements.summary: A short, quiet interlude in A-flat major, with no trumpets, trombones or timpani. Clarinets, violins and violas pass gentle songs between them, and a little rising four-note figure keeps nudging the music on. Schumann first called it an intermezzo.

mainIdeas.name: The first song
mainIdeas.description: a soft melody in the clarinets.

mainIdeas.name: The second song
mainIdeas.description: a warmer line in the violins.

mainIdeas.name: The third song
mainIdeas.description: a low, dark melody in the violas, with the cellos.

notice: Listen for the small rising figure of four quick notes that keeps reappearing, often at the end of a bar. It gives this calm movement a gentle forward push.

movements.heading: Feierlich
movements.summary: The cathedral movement. After a sharp chord, horns and trombones begin a slow, solemn theme in E-flat minor; the trombones have been silent until now. Schumann builds it up as strict [[counterpoint|counterpoint]], in the style of Bach: the theme enters in voice after voice, faster and slower, until it fills the orchestra like the sound of an organ under high vaults.

mainIdeas.name: The theme
mainIdeas.description: a slow, solemn line built from wide, hollow intervals.

mainIdeas.name: The interlude
mainIdeas.description: a short answering figure in the strings that keeps returning.

mainIdeas.name: The fanfare
mainIdeas.description: a bright call in the brass, near the end, in a far-off key.

movements.heading: Lebhaft
movements.summary: The doors open and the music steps out into daylight: a quick, light-footed finale in E-flat major, full of tunes. Near the end the solemn theme of the cathedral movement returns, now quick and bright, and the symphony ends in a dash.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 1
mainIdeas.description: a nimble, bouncing tune with lively accents, for the whole orchestra.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 2
mainIdeas.description: a crisp, detached tune in the strings.

mainIdeas.name: The memory
mainIdeas.description: the fourth movement’s solemn theme, transformed and festive.

threads.title: The Rhine and its cathedral
threads.body: The symphony grew out of Schumann’s first months in the Rhineland. The fourth movement remembers the great unfinished cathedral at Cologne, and the finale carries its theme back out into the streets.

threads.title: Five movements
threads.body: Between the dance (II) and the finale (V) Schumann places two slow movements of very different weight: a light interlude (III) and the solemn ceremony (IV).

threads.title: Music without titles
threads.body: He wrote descriptive headings and then removed them. He felt that once the eye is pointed at something, the ear can no longer judge freely.
